claims.text: The study concerns Q235 steel in its as-received, pre-exposure state.
Q235 samples will be annealed at 800 °C under oxygen partial pressures of 0.21 atm and 0.05 atm for the same duration.
Annealing Q235 steel in an oxygen-containing atmosphere will form a surface oxide scale.
A higher oxygen partial pressure during annealing will drive more rapid oxidation than a lower oxygen partial pressure.
Annealing at 0.21 atm oxygen will produce a denser, more continuous, and better-adhered oxide scale than annealing at 0.05 atm oxygen.
The protective oxide formed at high oxygen partial pressure may be a spinel phase.
A continuous surface film can improve corrosion protection.
The annealed oxide barrier will limit outward diffusion of Fe during high-temperature salt exposure.
The annealed oxide barrier will limit inward penetration of corrosive salt ions during high-temperature salt exposure.
Low-oxygen annealing will produce a porous or defective oxide scale.
A porous or defective oxide scale will be more susceptible to cracking and spallation under aggressive salt exposure.
High-oxygen-annealed samples will exhibit lower corrosion mass change than low-oxygen-annealed samples during exposure to Na2SO4–NaCl at 700–900 °C.
High-oxygen-annealed samples will exhibit fewer corrosion pits than low-oxygen-annealed samples.
High-oxygen annealing will enhance hardness and wear resistance during high-temperature salt exposure.
Room-temperature immersion tests will show minimal performance differences between the two annealing atmospheres.
The proposed protective mechanism is activated primarily by high-temperature oxidation kinetics in the range 700–900 °C.
The mechanism may not govern degradation when mechanical damage or non-oxidative corrosion mechanisms dominate.
Additional surface coatings can alter the oxidation behavior and make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Fluctuations in furnace atmosphere may cause variability in oxide quality.
Failure of high-oxygen annealing to produce a denser, better-adhered scale and statistically improved corrosion measurements relative to low-oxygen annealing would falsify the hypothesis.
